text: The Lord restored Job's losses when he prayed for his friends.
explanation:
Job's three friends had wounded him with accusations, and God was displeased with them. So He told them to bring an offering to Job and let Job pray for them. "And the Lord restored Job's losses when he prayed for his friends. Indeed the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before."

The turnaround came as Job turned his attention outward, and toward people who had hurt him. If you're waiting for your own breakthrough, pray for someone else's. Release the people who misjudged you. Restoration often comes through that door.

text: Don't judge God by the middle of Job's story. Look at the end: the Lord is very compassionate and merciful.
explanation:
"You have heard of the perseverance of Job and seen the end intended by the Lord: that the Lord is very compassionate and merciful." Job's 42 chapters can feel long, but most of it is conversation. His trial itself lasted months, not decades.

At the end, God blessed Job's latter days more than his beginning: twice the livestock, ten more children, and daughters more beautiful than any in the land. He lived another 140 years and saw four generations. Whatever chapter you're in, the end God intends for you is good.

text: Job's friends argued from experience, tradition and rules. Their words were partly true, but wrongly applied, and they only made things worse.
explanation:
Eliphaz argued from experience: "Who ever perished being innocent?… Even as I have seen." Bildad argued from tradition: "Inquire of the former age… consider the things discovered by their fathers." Zophar argued from legal logic: "If you would prepare your heart… if iniquity were in your hand, put it far away."

Their principles sounded right, but truth applied to the wrong person at the wrong time does harm. Their speeches only hardened Job. By chapter 29 he refers to himself over forty times and to God only a few. If you want to help a hurting friend, don't come with your experience, tradition or rules. Bring them God.

text: Job longed for a mediator who could lay one hand on God and one on him. You have one: Jesus.
explanation:
"Nor is there any mediator between us, who may lay his hand on us both," Job cried. In his day, there was no one to stand between a suffering man and a holy God and plead his case.

Today there is: "one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus." One of our own sits at the Father's right hand, a glorified Man whose heart still beats with human sympathy because He suffered as we do. Whatever you're going through, you have an Advocate in heaven.

text: "Deliver him from going down to the pit; I have found a ransom." Then: "His flesh shall be fresher than a child's."
explanation:
Elihu, the young man who spoke last, describes a person wasting away, bones sticking out, near the gates of death. Then: if a messenger, "one among a thousand," comes "to show man God's uprightness," not the man's own record, God is gracious and says, "Deliver him… I have found a ransom."

The result: "His flesh shall be young like a child's; he shall return to the days of his youth." God can be righteous in healing and restoring sinful people because He found a ransom: His own Son. Don't point a suffering person to their failures. Point them to the ransom.

text: Every time Satan moved against God's people, he ended up running into God, and serving God's purpose.
explanation:
He tempted Adam and Eve, and God announced the Seed who would crush his head. He sought to sift Peter like wheat, and Peter came out strengthened to strengthen his brothers. He accused and attacked Job, and Job ended up meeting God and being doubly blessed.

Above all, he thought the cross was his triumph over the Son of God, and the cross became the instrument that saved us all. The enemy thinks he's dealing with a weak saint, and keeps meeting a mighty God instead.

text: You don't have to wait until chapter 42. Say it now: "Lord, You are right. Everything I have is from You."
explanation:
Job's trouble exposed a root of self-righteousness in a genuinely good man: "I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame." When God finally spoke, He didn't list Job's faults; He showed His own majesty in creation. And Job said, "I have heard of You by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees You."

God disciplines His children with His word and sometimes with disappointing circumstances, but not with disease or disaster. Why take the long road? Agree with Him now. Drop the need to be right, in your marriage too, and you'll find a peace that self-justification never gives.
